blocks: The Handwriting on the Plaster: The Fall of Babylon, the Divine Balance Sheet, and the Righteousness of Christ
Sacrilege against known light, Heaven's marketplace audit, and the only weight that can cover us.
Big idea

On the night Babylon fell, God weighed a king who had sinned against what he knew, and ended his kingdom. John 5:22 says the Father has given all judgment to the Son. Jesus Christ is also the one who offers the only thing that can cover us when we are weighed: his own perfect righteousness.

In chapter 4, Nebuchadnezzar learned that Heaven rules. After seven years of living like an animal because of his pride, he lifted his eyes and blessed the Most High (Daniel 4:32–37). He published that confession to every nation. One generation later, Belshazzar sits in the same palace and acts as if the Most High does not exist.
Introduction
The Illusion of Invulnerability
Daniel 5:1–3 · Babylon, the night of the fall

In 539 B.C., the combined Medo-Persian army under Cyrus the Great and his general Ugbaru surrounded the city of Babylon. Outside the towering fortifications, an empire was crumbling; inside, King Belshazzar, who ruled in Babylon alongside his father Nabonidus (Main Point 1 explains), hosted a lavish, drunken banquet for a thousand of his highest nobles, along with his wives and concubines (Daniel 5:1–3).

Babylon was considered impregnable. Its monumental double walls were wide enough for multiple chariots to pass, and the Euphrates River ran directly beneath the water gates, providing an endless water supply and deep moats. Belshazzar saw no problem in having a party while the enemy surrounds the city. In an act of drunken insolence, he defied both the encircling armies outside and the God of heaven above.
Main Point 1
Belshazzar and the Historical Accuracy of Scripture

For a century, nineteenth-century critics claimed that the book of Daniel was historical fiction, and that Belshazzar never existed. Their reason was that the Greek historians and the Babylonian king lists named Nabonidus as the last king of Babylon and never mentioned a Belshazzar.
Archaeology has completely dismantled that skepticism:
The Nabonidus Cylinders of Ur

In 1854 J. G. Taylor dug up small clay cylinders written in cuneiform, the wedge-shaped writing of ancient Babylon. They hold a prayer by Nabonidus for his eldest son, "Bel-sar-usur," which is the Babylonian form of the name Belshazzar. So the king's son was real.
What an ancient Babylonian poem says about Nabonidus
Nabonidus made his home in Tema (also spelled Tayma), a desert town in Arabia, for ten years. He left the kingship and the defense of Babylon to his eldest son, Belshazzar.
The "third ruler" precision

Two men held power at the same time, a father and his son. This is called a co-regency. It explains why Belshazzar offered to make Daniel the "third ruler in the kingdom" (Daniel 5:16, 29). Nabonidus was first, Belshazzar was second, and the highest office left for Daniel was third.
1st Ruler
Nabonidus
King of Babylon, living in Tema (Tayma), Arabia.
Babylonian records place the king in Tema (Tayma) while the city is governed in his name. That absence is the reason a second man can hold the throne room on the night the writing appears.
2nd Ruler
Belshazzar
Eldest son and co-ruler, governing inside Babylon.

He offers the third place in the kingdom, not the second, and that is the detail the co-regency explains. In Daniel 5:7 the reward is to be the third ruler, which is what a son ruling under an absent father could actually grant.
3rd Ruler
Daniel
Offered the highest vacant post.
The reward is proclaimed and Daniel is clothed in scarlet the same night the city falls, and he takes it without asking for it. By morning the empire that offered it has changed hands.

HISTORY

Daniel 5 calls Nebuchadnezzar Belshazzar's "father" (Daniel 5:2, 11, 18, 22). In the Bible, "father" and "son" can mean an earlier and a later king of the same line, so "grandson" in this sitting means a later king of Nebuchadnezzar's dynasty, not necessarily a child's birth record. The chapter hangs on a king who knew the family lesson and still used God's cups to praise idols.
Main Point 2
The Anatomy of Sacrilege and Sinning Against Light

As the wine flowed, Belshazzar ordered the sacred gold and silver vessels taken by Nebuchadnezzar from Yahweh's temple in Jerusalem (Daniel 1:2) to be brought into the banquet hall. The king, his princes, his wives, and his concubines drank from those consecrated cups while singing praises to "the gods of gold, and of silver, of brass, of iron, of wood, and of stone" (Daniel 5:4).

This was not merely bad manners; it was deliberate sacrilege. He took what had been set apart for God and used it in a proud feast. Revelation later pictures Babylon as a woman arrayed in gold and precious stones, drunk with the blood of saints (Revelation 17:4–6). The parallel is that pattern: wealth used against what is holy, and against the saints.
Desecrating the consecrated
Sacrilege is taking that which has been set apart exclusively for the holy worship of God and dragging it into common, self-serving, or demonic usage.
Defying the living God
By praising idols using the very vessels designed for Yahweh's sanctuary, Belshazzar staged an intentional theological provocation, declaring Babylon's idols superior to the God of Israel.
Sinning against known revelation

When Daniel was summoned to read the writing on the wall (the next point explains it), he first gave the king a harsh charge (Daniel 5:18–23). Daniel reminded Belshazzar of how God had humbled his grandfather Nebuchadnezzar into the dust until he repented. Daniel looked the young monarch in the eyes and said: "And thou his son, O Belshazzar, hast not humbled thine heart, though thou knewest all this" (Daniel 5:22). Belshazzar's sin was worse because he knew better. "Light" here means knowledge of God. He had seen what happened to a proud king before him and chose not to learn from it. Luke 12:48 states the principle: "unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required." That is why judgment fell so swiftly.
Main Point 3
The Handwriting on the Plaster
The divine audit

The revelry halted abruptly when a mysterious hand appeared, writing on the plaster of the wall, over against the candlestick (Daniel 5:5). Belshazzar was terrified: the king's countenance was changed, and his thoughts troubled him, so that the joints of his loins were loosed, and his knees smote one against another (Daniel 5:6).

"In the same hour came forth fingers of a man's hand, and wrote over against the candlestick upon the plaister of the wall of the king's palace: and the king saw the part of the hand that wrote." — Daniel 5:5 (KJV)

The writing was four words: MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN (Daniel 5:25). MENE is written twice, and UPHARSIN means "and PARSIN," a form of PERES. These are Aramaic words, the everyday language of the empire. Daniel reads them as numbered, weighed, and divided (Daniel 5:26–28):
MENE (Numbered): The word sounds like the Aramaic word for counting. God has numbered the kingdom and finished it (Daniel 5:26). This throne’s account is closed in a night.
TEKEL (Weighed): The word sounds like the Aramaic word for weighing (the shekel is a weight). You have been placed upon the moral balances of divine justice and have been found wanting.
PERES (Divided): A wordplay in Aramaic: peres means "divided," and it sounds like Paras, the word for the Persians. The Babylonian Empire was to be dismantled and handed to the Medo-Persians.
TEXT

Every throne, institution, and individual life stands before an open ledger in Heaven. God numbers the days of power, weighs moral character, and — as at Belshazzar’s feast — can finish a kingdom in a night (Daniel 5:26–30).
Main Point 4
The Fall of Babylon and the Precision of Prophecy
Daniel 5:30 — “in that night”; 16 Tishri, 12 October 539 B.C.

That very night (Daniel 5:30), Babylon fell without a battle. Ugbaru’s troops entered on the sixteenth day of the month Tishri, 12 October 539 B.C. Persian engineers diverted the waters of the Euphrates River into an artificial basin. Persian soldiers marched down the depleted riverbed, passed through the bronze river gates left unlocked during the drunken festivities, and seized the palace.

That very night Belshazzar was slain, and Darius the Mede took the kingdom (Daniel 5:30–31). The Bible does not say how Darius relates to Cyrus, and the next sitting looks at that question. A Babylonian chronicle confirms the sudden fall: Ugbaru and the troops of Cyrus entered Babylon "without battle."

The gold kingdom gave way to the silver kingdom in a single evening. In the dream of Daniel 2, Babylon was the head of gold (Daniel 2:38), and a second kingdom, the chest and arms of silver (Daniel 2:32), was to come after it (Daniel 2:39). This reading takes that second kingdom to be Medo-Persia, so this night is that change.
Main Point 5
The Redemptive Core
Cyrus as type and Christ as the true Deliverer

The fall of Babylon is not merely an ancient political event. It is also a type: an earlier picture of a later act of God. Cyrus was named God's anointed, took Babylon, and freed the captives. Christ is the greater Anointed One, who frees his people from sin. Revelation uses the name Babylon for the final power that stands against God, and Revelation 18 shows that Babylon falling, as old Babylon fell.
Named God's "anointed" (Isa. 45:1)
Overthrew literal Babylon
Dried the waters of the Euphrates
Liberated Jewish captives without price
Commanded the rebuilding of Jerusalem
The true Anointed One, the Messiah
Overthrows the Babylon of Revelation 18
Frees captives, as Cyrus freed the exiles
Prepares a place; the New Jerusalem comes down
1. Cyrus, the anointed deliverer

God called Cyrus His "shepherd" (Isaiah 44:28) and His "anointed" (Hebrew: מָשִׁיחַ, Mashiach, Isaiah 45:1) — the only pagan ruler in Scripture to receive this title. Cyrus prefigured the Messiah by breaking the power of the oppressor, setting God's captive people free, and ordering the restoration of the temple (Isaiah 44:28; Isaiah 45:13). Isaiah wrote this in the days of King Hezekiah, more than a century before Cyrus took Babylon.
2. Christ, the ultimate Auditor and King

In John 5:22, Jesus declared: "For the Father judgeth no man, but hath committed all judgment unto the Son." The same Christ to whom the Father has committed all judgment will weigh every life (Revelation 20:11–12). Belshazzar’s night shows that Heaven already audits thrones.
3. Found wanting, yet covered by the righteousness Christ gives

Belshazzar was weighed and found wanting: "Thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting." The same verdict stands over everyone God weighs by his holy law, because "all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God" (Romans 3:23). Sin here means falling short of what God asks.
Here is the glory of the Gospel:
On the cross of Calvary, Jesus Christ bore the full weight of divine justice for our sins.

When a sinner repents and places their faith in Christ, His perfect righteousness is credited to our account (2 Corinthians 5:21; Romans 5:18–19). Righteousness means being right with God, and "credited" means counted as ours. Faith is how we accept this gift: Romans 4:5 says that to the one who "believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness."
When God weighs the believer, we are no longer found wanting; we possess the infinite, unassailable moral weight of the Son of God Himself.
CHRIST
If you stand in your own merit, you are found wanting. If you are clothed in the righteousness of Christ, you can stand before the throne with exceeding joy.
In plain words: God had already numbered, weighed, and divided Babylon, and the writing on the wall only announced the verdict.
INTERPRETATION

The writing on the plaster was not a prediction. It was a receipt. Babylon's end had already been decided, and the four Aramaic words announced a verdict that was complete before the hand appeared (Daniel 5:25-28).

Read the three words as a plain sequence. NUMBERED: God has counted the days this throne would last, and the count is finished. WEIGHED: the king himself was set on the scales against God's standard, and the standard did not move. DIVIDED: the kingdom was broken up and handed to another power that same night, which the words show by the sound of peres, close to Paras, the word for the Persians.

Why did this happen to this king, and not to another? Daniel tells him the reason to his face. Belshazzar knew what God had done to Nebuchadnezzar, and he did not humble his heart (Daniel 5:22). He took the cups that belonged to God's house and used them to praise gods of silver and gold (Daniel 5:23). So this was not an ordinary defeat in war. It was judgment on a man who had been handed the truth and treated it as a decoration.

The bottom line is uncomfortable and simple. Numbered, weighed and divided is how the chapter describes God's government of a life as well as of an empire. To be numbered is to admit your days are not your own to spend. To be weighed is to admit your own merit will not balance the account. That is why this book turns, in every sitting, to One whose righteousness is given rather than earned.
Practical Application
Navigating the Feasts of Modern Babylon
Belshazzar's downfall provides sobering warnings for the modern world:
Beware of feasting on borrowed holy things

The world takes what belongs to God, such as truth, time, and worship, and treats it as a plaything for selfish pleasure. God will not be mocked; whatever a man sows, that shall he also reap (Galatians 6:7).
Do not presume upon past mercy

Belshazzar knew what God had done to Nebuchadnezzar and presumed he could escape judgment. He did not humble his heart (Daniel 5:22), and that refusal was the charge against him. Truth that we know and ignore counts against us in the same way.
Anchor your life in Christ's righteousness
Worldly security can vanish overnight, just as Babylon fell in a single hour (Revelation 18:10). The only refuge from the divine scale is the righteousness of Jesus Christ.
The principle to remember
God weighs every throne and every life, and only the righteousness of Christ can cover what is found wanting. Test any reading with four questions:
TEXT — Does Daniel 5:22 say Belshazzar knew all this and still did not humble his heart?
HISTORY — Do the ancient Babylonian records confirm the co-regency and a fall "without battle"?
INTERPRETATION — Are MENE, TEKEL, and PERES the verbs numbered, weighed, and divided?
CHRIST — Does the scale find you wanting in yourself, or covered by the righteousness of the Son?
The Auditor Who Weighs — and the Righteousness That Covers

Daniel 5:5 names fingers of a man's hand, not Jesus. John 5:22 still holds: the Father has committed all judgment unto the Son. Belshazzar was found wanting because he sinned against light he already possessed (Daniel 5:22).

Cyrus, named God's anointed (Isaiah 45:1). This sitting's reading: he is a type of the true Messiah. Isaiah 44:27 says the deep would be dry; 45:1 names the two leaved gates. Christ overthrows spiritual Babylon (Revelation 18), conquers sin, conquers death (1 Corinthians 15:26), and the New Jerusalem comes down from God (Revelation 21:2).

On our own merit the verdict is TEKEL — found wanting. On the cross Christ bore the full weight of justice; His righteousness is credited to the believer (2 Corinthians 5:21). When God weighs those who trust the Son, they possess the moral weight of Christ Himself.
Next lesson
